1	\chapter{The \'etale plus construction of the relative Picard functor}
2	\label{chap:PicardEtale}
3	
4	For a curve \(C\) over \(k\) and an affine test scheme \(\Spec A\), the \'etale-sheafified
5	relative Picard group is computed by a single \emph{plus construction}: a class is represented
6	by a relative Picard class on an \'etale cover of \(\Spec A\) satisfying a descent condition,
7	and two representatives are identified when they agree on a common refinement. This chapter
8	constructs that plus, on affine test schemes indexed by a \(k\)-algebra \(A\); we recall from
9	elsewhere in this project the ambient functor it sheafifies. For an object \(T\) of
10	\(\Over(\Spec k)\) write \(\mathrm{relPic}(C,T)\) for the relative Picard group of \(C\) at
11	\(T\) --- the quotient of the Picard group of \(C \otimes T\) by the subgroup of classes pulled
12	back from \(T\) along the second projection --- a commutative group, with restriction
13	homomorphisms \(g^{*} \colon \mathrm{relPic}(C,T) \to \mathrm{relPic}(C,T')\) for a morphism
14	\(g \colon T' \to T\) of \(\Over(\Spec k)\), satisfying \((\id_T)^{*} = \id\) and
15	\((g \circ h)^{*} = h^{*} \circ g^{*}\). For a commutative \(k\)-algebra \(A\), write \(\Spec A\)
16	also for the object of \(\Over(\Spec k)\) it determines via the structure morphism
17	\(\Spec A \to \Spec k\) induced by the \(k\)-algebra structure of \(A\); a homomorphism of
18	\(k\)-algebras \(A \to A'\) induces, via \(\Spec\), a morphism \(\Spec A' \to \Spec A\) of
19	\(\Over(\Spec k)\). We abbreviate \(\mathrm{relPic}(C,A) := \mathrm{relPic}(C,\Spec A)\).
20	
21	\section{Presented \'etale covers of an affine scheme}
22	
23	Throughout this section \(A\) is a commutative ring (no field or \(k\)-algebra structure is
24	needed here). An \'etale cover of \(\Spec A\) in the sense consumed by the plus construction is
25	a faithfully flat \'etale \(A\)-algebra; to keep the index of covers of a fixed base
26	small --- which is what makes the plus construction below a legitimate colimit, rather than one
27	indexed by a proper class of isomorphism types --- we realize such algebras through an explicit
28	finite-variable presentation, at the cost of carrying a witness of the presentation as data.
29	
30	\begin{definition}[Presented \'etale cover]
31	  \label{def:etale_cover}
32	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover, Algebra.EtaleCover.Carrier}
33	  \leanok
34	  A \emph{presented \'etale cover} \(E\) of \(A\) consists of a natural number \(n\), an ideal
35	  \(I\) of the polynomial ring \(A[x_1,\dots,x_n]\), a proof that the quotient algebra
36	  \(B_E := A[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I\) is \'etale over \(A\), and a proof that the induced map of
37	  spectra \(\Spec B_E \to \Spec A\) is surjective. We call \(B_E\) the \emph{carrier} of \(E\).
38	  Since \'etale algebras are flat, surjectivity of \(\Spec B_E \to \Spec A\) together with
39	  flatness makes \(B_E\) faithfully flat over \(A\).
40	\end{definition}
41	
42	\begin{definition}[Presented covers from an \'etale algebra]
43	  \label{def:etale_cover_of}
44	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover.of}
45	  \uses{def:etale_cover}
46	  \leanok
47	  Let \(B\) be an \'etale \(A\)-algebra such that \(\Spec B \to \Spec A\) is surjective. Since
48	  \'etale algebras are of finite presentation, \(B\) admits a presentation as a quotient of a
49	  polynomial ring in finitely many variables over \(A\); choosing one such presentation
50	  produces a presented \'etale cover \(E\) of \(A\), denoted \(E = \mathrm{of}(B)\).
51	\end{definition}
52	
53	\begin{lemma}[Carrier of a presented cover from an algebra]
54	  \label{lem:etale_cover_ofEquiv}
55	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover.ofEquiv}
56	  \uses{def:etale_cover_of}
57	  \leanok
58	  In the situation of Definition~\ref{def:etale_cover_of}, the carrier \(B_E\) of
59	  \(E = \mathrm{of}(B)\) is isomorphic to \(B\) as an \(A\)-algebra.
60	\end{lemma}
61	\begin{proof}
62	  \leanok
63	  Immediate from the construction: \(E\) is built from a chosen presentation
64	  \(A[x_1,\dots,x_n] \twoheadrightarrow B\), and the carrier of the resulting cover is the
65	  quotient of \(A[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) by the kernel of that presentation, which is isomorphic to
66	  \(B\) by the first isomorphism theorem for algebras.
67	\end{proof}
68	
69	\begin{definition}[Refinement]
70	  \label{def:etale_cover_refines}
71	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover.Refines}
72	  \uses{def:etale_cover}
73	  \leanok
74	  For presented \'etale covers \(E, E'\) of \(A\), we say \(E'\) \emph{refines} \(E\) if there
75	  exists a homomorphism of \(A\)-algebras \(B_E \to B_{E'}\) (equivalently, a morphism
76	  \(\Spec B_{E'} \to \Spec B_E\) over \(\Spec A\)). This is a mere existence statement: no
77	  particular refinement map is remembered as data.
78	\end{definition}
79	
80	\begin{lemma}[Refinement is a preorder]
81	  \label{lem:etale_cover_refines_preorder}
82	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover.refines_refl, Algebra.EtaleCover.Refines.trans}
83	  \uses{def:etale_cover_refines}
84	  \leanok
85	  Every presented \'etale cover \(E\) of \(A\) refines itself, and if \(E''\) refines \(E'\)
86	  and \(E'\) refines \(E\) then \(E''\) refines \(E\).
87	\end{lemma}
88	\begin{proof}
89	  \leanok
90	  Reflexivity: the identity homomorphism of \(B_E\) witnesses that \(E\) refines itself.
91	  Transitivity: composing a homomorphism \(B_{E'} \to B_{E''}\) witnessing that \(E''\) refines
92	  \(E'\) with a homomorphism \(B_E \to B_{E'}\) witnessing that \(E'\) refines \(E\) gives a
93	  homomorphism \(B_E \to B_{E''}\) witnessing that \(E''\) refines \(E\).
94	\end{proof}
95	
96	\begin{definition}[Common refinement]
97	  \label{def:etale_cover_prod}
98	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover.prod, Algebra.EtaleCover.prodEquiv}
99	  \uses{def:etale_cover_of}
100	  \leanok
101	  For presented \'etale covers \(E, E'\) of \(A\), the \emph{common refinement} \(E \times E'\)
102	  is the presented \'etale cover of \(A\) with carrier \(B_E \otimes_A B_{E'}\) (\'etale over
103	  \(A\) because it is \'etale over the \'etale algebra \(B_E\), which is \'etale over \(A\); and
104	  faithfully flat by transitivity of faithfully flat extensions), obtained by applying
105	  Definition~\ref{def:etale_cover_of} to \(B_E \otimes_A B_{E'}\).
106	\end{definition}
107	
108	\begin{definition}[Coprojections of the common refinement]
109	  \label{def:etale_cover_prod_coproj}
110	  \lean{Algebra.EtaleCover.prodInl, Algebra.EtaleCover.prodInr}
111	  \uses{def:etale_cover_prod}
112	  \leanok
113	  The two canonical homomorphisms of \(A\)-algebras
114	  \(B_E \to B_{E \times E'} \cong B_E \otimes_A B_{E'}\), \(b \mapsto b \otimes 1\), and
115	  \(B_{E'} \to B_{E \times E'}\), \(b' \mapsto 1 \otimes b'\), transported along the carrier
116	  identification of Definition~\ref{def:etale_cover_prod}.
117	\end{definition}
118	
119	\begin{lemma}[The common refinement refines both factors]
120	  \label{lem:etale_cover_prod_refines}

1261	Finally, there are two appendices.  Appendix A contains detailed answers
1262	to all the exercises.  Appendix B develops basic divisorial intersection
1263	theory, which is used freely throughout Section 6.  The treatment is
1264	short, simple, and elementary.
1265	
1266	\section{The several Picard functors}\label{sc:Pfctrs}
1267	\renewcommand{\theequation}{\thethm.\arabic{equation}}
1268	Our first job is to identify a likely candidate for the functor of
1269	points of the Picard scheme.  In fact, there are several reasonable such
1270	Picard functors, and each one is more likely to be representable than
1271	the preceding.  In this section, they all are formally introduced and
1272	compared.
1273	
1274	\begin{dfn}\label{df:aPf}
1275	 The {\it absolute Picard functor} $\Pic_X$ is the functor from  the
1276	 category of (locally Noetherian) $S$-schemes $T$ to the category of
1277	abelian groups defined by the formula
1278		$$\Pic_X(T):=\Pic(X_T).$$
1279	\end{dfn}
1280	
1281	The absolute Picard functor  is a ``prepared presheaf'' in this
1282	sense: given any family of  $S$-schemes $T_i$, we have
1283		$$\Pic_X\bigl(\textstyle\coprod T_i\bigr)=\prod\Pic_X(T_i).$$
1284	 Hence, given a covering family $\{T_i\to T\}$ in the Zariski topology,
1285	the \'etale topology, or any other Grothendieck topology on the category
1286	of $S$-schemes, there is no harm, when we consider the sheaf associated
1287	to $\Pic_X$, in working simply with the single map $T'\to T$ where
1288	$T':=\coprod T_i$.  And doing so lightens the notation, making for
1289	easier reading. Therefore, we do so throughout, calling $T'\to T$ simply
1290	a {\it covering\/} in the given topology.
1291	
1292	The absolute Picard functor $\Pic_X$ is never a separated presheaf in
1293	the Zariski topology.  Indeed, take an $S$-scheme $T$ that carries an
1294	invertible sheaf $\mc N$ such that $f^*_T\mc N$ is nontrivial.  (For
1295	example, take $T:=\I P^1_X$ and $\mc N:=\mc O_{\!T}(1)$.  Then the diagonal
1296	map $X\to X\x X$ induces a section $g$ of $f_T$; that is, $gf_T=1_T$.
1297	Hence $f^*_T\mc N$ is nontrivial.)  Now, there exists a Zariski covering
1298	$T'\to T$ such that the pullback $\mc N|T'$ is trivial; here, $T'$ is
1299	simply the disjoint union of the subsets in a suitable ordinary open
1300	covering of $T$.  So the pullback $f^*_{T'}\mc N|X_{T'}$ is trivial too.
1301	Thus $\Pic_X(T)$ has a nonzero element whose restriction is zero in
1302	$\Pic_X(T')$.
1303	
1304	According to descent theory, every representable functor is a sheaf in
1305	the Zariski topology \emdash in fact, in the \'etale and fppf
1306	topologies as well.  Therefore, the absolute Picard functor $\Pic_X$ is never
1307	representable.  So, in the hope of obtaining a representable functor
1308	that differs as little as possible from $\Pic_X$, we now define a
1309	sequence of three successively more promising relative functors.
1310	
1311	\begin{dfn}\label{df:Pfs}
1312	  The {\it relative Picard functor} $\Pic_{X/S}$ is defined by
1313		$$\Pic_{X/S}(T):=\Pic(X_T)\big/\Pic(T).$$
1314	 Denote its associated sheaves in the Zariski, \'etale, and fppf
1315	topologies  by
1316		$$\Pic_{(X/S)\zar},\ \Pic_{(X/S)\et},\
1317		\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}.$$
1318	 \end{dfn}
1319	
1320	We now have a sequence of five Picard functors, and each one maps
1321	naturally into the next.  So each one maps naturally into any of its
1322	successors.  If the latter functor is one of the three just displayed,
1323	then it is a sheaf in the indicated topology; in fact, it is the sheaf
1324	associated to any one of its predecessors, and the map between them is
1325	the natural map from a presheaf to its associated sheaf, as is easy to
1326	check.  In particular, the three displayed sheaves are the sheaves
1327	associated to the absolute Picard functor $\Pic_X$, as well as to the
1328	relative Picard functor $\Pic_{X/S}$.
1329	
1330	Since $\Pic_{X/S}$ is not a priori a sheaf, it is remarkable that it is
1331	representable so often in practice.
1332	
1333	Note that, for every $S$-scheme $T$, each $T$-point of
1334	$\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}$, or element of $\Pic_{(X/S)\fpqc}(T)$, is
1335	represented by an invertible sheaf $\mc L'$ on $X_{T'}$ for some
1336	fppf-covering $T'\to T$.    Moreover, there must
1337	be an fppf-covering $T''\to T'\x_T T'$ such that the two pullbacks of
1338	$\mc L'$ to $X_{T''}$ are isomorphic \emdash or to put it informally, the
1339	restrictions of $\mc L'$ must agree on a covering of the overlaps.
1340	
1341	Furthermore, a second such sheaf $\mc L_1$ on $X_{T_1}$ represents the
1342	same $T$-point if and only if there is an fppf-covering $T_1'\to T_1\x_T
1343	T'$ such that the pullbacks of $\mc L'$ and $\mc L_1$ to $X_{T_1'}$ are
1344	isomorphic.  Technically, this condition includes the preceding one,
1345	which concerns the case where $T_1=T'$ and $\mc L_1=\mc L'$ since $\mc
1346	L'$ must represent the same $T$-point as itself.  Of course, similar
1347	considerations apply to the Picard functors for the Zariski and \'etale
1348	topologies as well.
1349	
1350	\begin{ex}\label{ex:Alr}
1351	 Given an $S$-scheme $T$ of the form $T=\Spec(A)$ where $A$ is a local
1352	ring, show that the natural maps are isomorphisms
1353		$$\Pic_X(A)\risom\Pic_{X/S}(A)\risom\Pic_{(X/S)\zar}(A)$$
1354	 where $\Pic_X(A):=\Pic_X(T)$, where $\Pic_{X/S}(A):=\Pic_{X/S}(T)$,
1355	and so forth.
1356	
1357	Assume $A$ is Artin local with algebraically closed residue field.  Show
1358		$$\Pic_X(A)\risom\Pic_{(X/S)\et}(A).$$
1359	
1360	Assume $A$ is an algebraically closed  field $k$.  Show
1361		$$\Pic_X(k)\risom\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}(k).$$
1362	  \end{ex}
1363	
1364	\begin{ex}\label{ex:Pfs}
1365	 Show that the natural map
1366		$$\Pic_{(X/S)\zar}\to \Pic_{(X/S)\et}$$
1367	 need not be an isomorphism.  Specifically, take $X$ to be the following
1368	 curve  in the real projective plane:
1369		$$X:u^2+v^2+w^2=0 \text{ in }\I P^2_\bb R.$$
1370	 Then $X$ has no $\bb R$-points, but  over the complex numbers $\bb C$,
1371	 there is an isomorphism
1372		$$\vf\:X_{\bb C}\risom\I P^1_{\bb C}.$$
1373	 Show that $\vf^*\mc O(1)$ defines an element of $\Pic_{(X/\bb R)\et}(\bb
1374	R)$, which is not in the image of $\Pic_{(X/\bb R)\zar}(\bb R)$.
1375	 \end{ex}
1376	
1377	The main result of this section is the following comparison theorem.
1378	It identifies two useful conditions: the first guarantees that the first
1379	three relative functors can be viewed as subfunctors of the fourth;
1380	together, the two conditions guarantee that all four functors coincide.
1381	The second condition has three successively weaker forms.  Before we can
1382	prove the theorem, we must develop some theory.
1383	
1384	\begin{thm}[Comparison]\label{th:cmp}
1385	 Assume $\mc O_{\!S}\risom f_*\mc O_{\!X}$ holds universally; that is, for any
1386	$S$-scheme $T$, the comorphism of $f_T$ is an isomorphism, $\mc O_{\!T}\risom
1387	f_{\smash{T}*}\mc O_{\!X_T}$.
1388	 \smallskip
1389	
1390	\tu{1.}\enspace
1391	 Then the natural maps are injections:
1392		$$\Pic_{X/S}\into \Pic_{(X/S)\zar}\into \Pic_{(X/S)\et}\into
1393		\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}.$$
1394	
1395	\tu{2.}\enspace All three maps are isomorphisms if also $f$ has a
1396	section; the latter two maps are isomorphisms if also $f$ has a section
1397	locally in the Zariski topology; and the last map is isomorphism if also
1398	$f$ has a section locally in the \'etale topology.
1399	 \end{thm}
1400	
1401	\begin{ex}\label{ex:gpts}
1402	 Assume $\mc O_{\!S}\risom f_*\mc O_{\!X}$ holds universally.  Using
1403	Theorem~\ref{th:cmp}, show that its four functors  have the same
1404	geometric points; in other words, for every algebraically closed field
1405	$k$ containing the residue class field of a point of $S$, the $k$-points
1406	of all four functors are, in a natural way, the same.  Show, in fact,
1407	that these $k$-points are just the elements of $\Pic(X_k)$.
1408	
1409	What if $\mc O_{\!S}\risom f_*\mc O_{\!X}$ does not necessarily hold
1410	universally?
1411	 \end{ex}
1412	
1413	\begin{lem}\label{lm:fff}

106	  \(T^j \cdot x \in Q_0 + Q_1 + \langle F \rangle_k\), where \(\langle F \rangle_k\) is the
107	  \(k\)-submodule generated by \(F\).
108	
109	  Indeed, if \(j \ge 0\), then since \(x \in s \subseteq Q_0\) and \(Q_0\) is stable under
110	  \(T\), Lemma~\ref{lem:T_pow_stable} gives \(T^j \cdot x \in Q_0\). If \(j \le -M\), write
111	  \(j = -d - M\) with \(d = -j - M \ge 0\); then
112	  \[
113	    T^j \cdot x = T^{-d} \cdot \bigl(T^{-M} \cdot x\bigr) ,
114	  \]
115	  and since \(T^{-M} \cdot x \in Q_1\) and \(Q_1\) is stable under \(T^{-1}\),
116	  Lemma~\ref{lem:T_inv_pow_stable} gives \(T^j \cdot x \in Q_1\). Finally, if \(-M < j < 0\),
117	  then \(T^j \cdot x \in F \subseteq \langle F \rangle_k\) by definition of \(F\). This proves
118	  the claim.
119	
120	  Every element \(f \in k[T,T^{-1}]\) is, by definition of the Laurent polynomial ring, a
121	  \(k\)-linear combination of finitely many monomials \(T^j\), \(j \in \Z\). Since
122	  \(Q_0 + Q_1 + \langle F \rangle_k\) is a \(k\)-submodule of \(N\), the claim and this
123	  decomposition of \(f\) give, for every \(x \in s\),
124	  \[

126	  \]

129	  in \(Q_0 + Q_1 + \langle F \rangle_k\) by the previous paragraph, and this submodule is
130	  closed under addition, so \(n \in Q_0 + Q_1 + \langle F \rangle_k\). Hence
131	  \[

133	  \]

135	  N/(Q_0+Q_1)\) is surjective, so the (finite) image of \(F\) in \(N/(Q_0+Q_1)\) spans it as a
136	  \(k\)-module. Thus \(N/(Q_0+Q_1)\) is a finite \(k\)-module.
137	\end{proof}

142	localization-type hypothesis on \(Q_0\) is available, symmetric to hypothesis (5) on \(Q_1\):

144	large power of \(T\). The next two results derive the finiteness conclusion from this
145	symmetric pair of hypotheses, at the cost of assuming \(N\) itself is a finite

147	finite module away from an element.

163	      with \(T^{-m} \cdot n \in Q_1\).

1	\chapter{Lattice finiteness over the Laurent ring}
2	\label{chap:Algebra}
3	
4	This chapter isolates a general finiteness lemma about pairs of lattices in a module over
5	the ring of Laurent polynomials. Write \(k[T, T^{-1}]\) for the ring of Laurent polynomials
6	over a commutative ring \(k\) (Chapter~\ref{chap:Curves}): the free \(k\)-module on the
7	monomials \(T^n\), \(n \in \Z\), with multiplication \(T^m \cdot T^n = T^{m+n}\), so that
8	\(T^0 = 1\) and \(T^{-1}\) is a two-sided inverse of \(T\). For a subset \(s\) of a
9	\(k[T,T^{-1}]\)-module \(N\), write \(\langle s \rangle_{k[T,T^{-1}]}\) for the
10	\(k[T,T^{-1}]\)-submodule it generates. Call a \(k\)-module \emph{finite} if it is finitely
11	generated over \(k\), and for \(k\)-submodules \(Q_0, Q_1\) of a \(k\)-module, write
12	\(Q_0 + Q_1\) for the smallest \(k\)-submodule containing both.
13	
14	The result abstracts the classical computation, for the projective line covered by its two
15	standard affine charts, of the cohomology of a coherent sheaf as the cokernel of the
16	difference-of-restrictions map out of the two chart section rings into the ring of sections
17	on the overlap: two \(k\)-submodules \(Q_0, Q_1\) of a \(k[T,T^{-1}]\)-module \(N\), one
18	stable under multiplication by \(T\) and containing enough of \(N\), the other stable under
19	multiplication by \(T^{-1}\) and eventually absorbing every element of \(N\), leave a quotient
20	\(N / (Q_0 + Q_1)\) that is a finite \(k\)-module — because only a finite window of monomials
21	can fail to be absorbed by one lattice or the other.

29	  \label{lem:T_pow_stable}
